Attorney Alyssa Holmes appeared for plaintiff. Motion for service by publication ALLOWED. Counsel to contact Attorney Leo Bieler in the office of the Recorder to arrange for publication of a citation as to two defendant entities, no longer in legal existence, and their successors. Following return dates on all summonses and the published citation, plaintiff to request default enter under Mass. R. Civ. P. 55 (a) against all parties not timely filing answer or 55 (b) (2) for default judgment (with affidavit(s) and/or brief legal memorandum demonstrating entitlement to relief sought, and proposed form of judgment). Alternatively, if any additional party appears or answers, parties promptly to request, in writing, further case management conference. (Piper, C.J.)  (Notice of Docket Entry sent to Attorneys Alyssa Holmes and Stephanie Sprague)

Ex parte hearing held on the plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order and/or preliminary injunction. Plaintiffs Kristin L. Croci and Gretchen K. Porter, as trustees of the C and N Family Realty Trust, appeared through counsel, ex parte. After hearing arguments from the plaintiffs, the Court DENIES the motion, but GRANTS their request for a hearing on short notice. The Court ORDERS the parties to appear on August 25, 2023 at 12:00 PM, at the Land Court in Boston, for a hearing on the plaintiffs' motion. The Court DIRECTS the plaintiffs to promptly  serve this order by email on defendants' counsel and file a return of service. SO ORDERED.

row.description: Defendant's motion to dismiss-While the grand jury minutes on page 9 indicate that Inv. Kirchner used the feminine pronoun "her" when referring to the person who entered the house to retrieve the gun, it seems readily apparent that he either misspoke or t hat there is an error in the transcription of the minutes. I reach that conclusion because subsequent questioning by both the prosecutor and the grand jurors made it clear that no one believed or suggested that the defendant ever had the gun in her hand. If Inv. Kirchner did misspeak, h is action was, at worse negligence, and did not constitute intentional or reckless conduct. Moreover, in light of the tenor of the subsequent questioning, I do not believe that his misstatement made a difference in the grand jury's decision to indict. See Commonwealth v. Mayfield, 398 Mass. 615, 621-622 (1986). With respect to the testimony given on pages 14 and 15 of the grand jury minutes, it is true that Krupa did not expressly say in his written statement that the defendant was aware of the transaction. However, he said enough to warrant such an inference. A prosecutor is not required to present all exculpatory evidence to a grand jury, but she "must disclose evidence that would greatly undermine the credibility of evidence likely to affect the gran jury's decision to indict." Commonwealth v. Ali, 43 Mass.App.Ct. 549, 557 (1997). I do not believe that Krupa's written statement greatly undermined the credibility of the evidence presented, or that the failure to present that statement to the grand jury affected their decision to indict. I take a dim view of Inv. Kirchner's editorial comment on page 15: "Unless she's wearing earplugs or blindfolded." Police officers testifying before a grand jury should recite the facts, not offer their opinions (unless, of course, they are giving proper expert testimony). However, even though the imporper portion of the witness's answer would be inadmmissible at trial, it was generally responsive to a grand juror's question. See Commonwealth v. Freeman, 407 Mass. 279, 284 (1990). It therefore appears that the prosecutor and the witness did not undertake to present that opinion to the grand jury in order to procure an indictment. See Commonwealth v. Champagne, 399 Mass. 80, 84 (1987). Finally, having in mind that the standard at this stage is probable cause and not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, I conclude that the evidence presented to the grand jury, while thin, was sufficient to support the indictments. Accordingly, the motion is Denied (Ford, J.).
